chapter: Army service and the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
title: Verdun, Harry Truman, Pershing and the return from Le Havre
summary: White tells of concerts at Verdun, serenading Truman, the Montfaucon cemetery with General Pershing, his status as bandmaster, and the wait in Le Havre.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well, then began the history of the 816th Band. Well, the history of the 816th Band measures up very creditably. In that while we were stationed in Verdun, every afternoon except Saturday and Sundays, we had to play a concert in Chevert Square in Verdun. Aside from other planes that we did around in various camps, I serenaded Harry Truman over there, his regiment, Captain Harry Truman. But I didn't know it was Captain Harry Truman. I knew it was Captain Harry Truman there, but I heard no more about him until he became senator, United States Senator. When we arrived out of the camp with the two truckloads of instruments and the two truckload load of band and jumped out while he was sitting at the piano playing.

Yeah, sure. Yeah, sure. And so, when we walked in, I said, I'm reporting from the 816th Finan Enfrager on the orders of Colonel Chaplin to come up here and serenade you. He said, hell, we don't need any serenading up here. I'll do it to serenade. He said, go on back there and get you something to eat and you can go on back to camp. Oh, he's a wonderful guy, you know. That's why I love him until today. He was so forthright. Great man. But, back to the regiment of band activities. Now, when they started building this big cemetery out from Burden in a little town called Montfaucon, Romaine, a little town just beyond Montfaucon where the cemetery presently is situated now, I suppose, if it hasn't been demolished. Why, we were stationed up there for, from March the 8th until June the 8th. And then the construction of this cemetery, now, my band was never called to do any work in the work. All we were required to do was to entertain the boys and we were given our company street and company barracks. We put up our big tents and I had the tent at the head of the barracks and here was the Colonel's quarters down here. And, I dined with the, in the Colonel's quarters, not with the Colonel and the staff, but I dined in his quarters. The better, higher non-commissioned officers all dined over there. A little better service too, strange to say. I don't want to be different from the men, create a little jealousy. But, that, that was the way it was handled. I had to obey the orders of the, of the other higher non-coms. Of course, I was the highest non-com in my regiment. I was acting warrant officer. I was never commissioned, however. But, I drew the salary of a warrant officer and I had the power of a warrant officer. Mine was only as an assistant bandmaster. That's the rank, permanent rank. That's the discharge rank too. Because, no commission was ever signed and you don't go over the commissions. But, I was the bandmaster, the recognized bandmaster. And, I had no other bandmaster over me at any time. I had no other officer over me. All my conducting of my band over there was done with, with me alone as the sole arbiter of anything. I serenaded, uh, General John J. Pershing four times. But, the ground breaking for the cemetery building, he was there. My band sat right under the stand. My band did the salutation number for his entry. At the closing, my band played the Stars and Stripes and the French national anthem. The French national anthem first and the Stars and Stripes last in France. At the conclusion of this cemetery, General Pershing was up there again to set the flag up and acclaim the cemetery, the largest in the world. And, this was a big day. On the 8th day of June, 1919. And, again, my band was a host band to General John J. Pershing. Now then, right after that, we were supposed to go down and take his band's place at Shawmont. But, orders from General Smedley D. Butler, uh, at La Havre, changed the orders. He set the order that the 816 Pioneer Infantry would sail in August for the United States. When we got to La Havre, France, my General Smedley D. Butler proclaimed, this band is now the Army Camps Band and you are disassociated with the 816 Pioneer Infantry. That's when Maurice left me and went to the hospital. Well, we, each day, our only requirements, whether we play a concert in the Y at a little afternoon or before noon, sometimes early in the morning. I got all my orders from him, typewritten orders. Your band will entrain today and play for so-and-so and so-and-so and so-and-so. Such, uh, dignitaries would be arriving, you know, and the soldiers were in training for home. Uh, then, you would proceed down to the docks today at 2.30, and there you will stand guard and play for the sailing of troops home until 8 o'clock tonight. So, you see, my band had unusual privileges down in La Havre. And, and during the loading of a ship here and the sailing of that ship, and another ship would come in and another bunch of soldiers would come in, they had lead. So, they'd run all around the town. And some of them came back with saxoconiac. We had a very good time there. And my boys was very obedient to every wish of mine. While they were beating up other bandmasters over there, and they threw one overboard coming back. Really? They threw one bandmaster over the ship. And then it was, they, they'd whip up a bandmaster in a minute. Especially if you were a non-commissioned bandmaster, you didn't have any voice. They'd whip up an officer for that matter. They were mad to come home. But my band was just as jubilant over coming home. But yet, well, I had to be somewhat conciliatory with them, you know. Well, you'll be home pretty soon. I wonder if they're going to keep us in the army. Some of them would say, I said, oh no, you'll be mustered out as soon as you get over there. Little did I think that that would be done, but that was my word to them. And sure enough, well, we came back safe. We gave a concert on the ship, coming back every day. We got back in 11 days. But we stayed in La Hava down there for a solid 24 days. And, yeah, and we had a wonderful time there in La Hava. After I got my discharge in Louisville, Kentucky, I headed down to New Orleans. Because I knew JC Miles had passed. And I knew Lizzie down there. And I didn't know anybody else much in America where I wanted to go. And so I went down to New Orleans. It wasn't with the idea that I'd go down to wait anybody. That's completely out of the question. But I went down there because I had a friend down there. And I still consider her one of my greatest friends. But she is so, she's such a devout Catholic and a good Christian person. That's right. And it would be shameless for me to say anything different about her. She befriended me so many times. And even while she was out here. And I got some letters back there. Letters as late as 1957, the last letters. Just the early part of last year when she had been to the Tin Angel over there. But she had gone back home to take care of her home. And, uh...
